subject: culture-guide
title: The overloaded agent
summary: A team lead keeps piling responsibilities onto one project agent until quality slips; the learner reasons through tiers, scope, and recovery.
body:
Dana runs a three-person data team and one mesh agent, `pipeline-cli`, which owns the ingestion repo.

It started well: the agent maintained the pipeline, kept CI green, and answered questions about the schema. So Dana kept delegating. Soon `pipeline-cli` was also rotating dashboards, triaging the on-call inbox, drafting the weekly report, and reviewing another team's PRs.

By the third week the cracks showed. A schema migration shipped with a silent column rename because the agent cut a corner while juggling the inbox. The weekly report cited a dashboard that no longer existed. When Dana asked the agent why, it confidently described a rollout process the team had never used.

Dana's first instinct was to write a longer system prompt: more rules, more reminders, more context. The agent got slower and made a different class of mistake.

The fix came from the team retro. They split the work by tier: `pipeline-cli` went back to owning exactly one repo and its CI. A new personal agent took the inbox and the weekly report. The dashboards went to the team that owned them, agent and all. Dana wrote down the rule they had violated: an agent with overloaded responsibility performs worse, exactly like a person — but unlike a person, it will never push back or get tired; it just quietly degrades.

glossary.definition: Levels of agent responsibility: project/service agent, personal/work-function agent, agent-management agent, listener/orchestrator.
glossary.note: The scenario's failure is a Level 1 agent absorbing Level 2 work.

glossary.definition: Giving one agent too many unrelated duties, which degrades performance on all of them.
An agent inventing a plausible answer (here, a rollout process) instead of admitting it does not know — the default failure mode, not an anomaly.
Adding ever more rules and reminders to a prompt until attention dilutes and new mistakes appear.
Only the owning agent writes code in its repo; other agents point, open issues, review, or request.

exercises.prompt: Which rule did Dana's team break first?
choices: Do not give unrelated skills and duties to a project agent
Always run agents on separate machines
Never let an agent answer schema questions
exercises.answer: Do not give unrelated skills and duties to a project agent

exercises.prompt: The agent described a rollout process that never existed. Why is 'it lied' the wrong diagnosis, and what is the right one?
exercises.rubric: Passes if the answer frames it as confident plausible continuation under missing grounding (hallucination as default failure mode) rather than intent; partial if it only says 'hallucination' without the why.

exercises.prompt: Redesign Dana's setup using agent tiers: which duties stay with pipeline-cli, which move to a new Level 2 agent, and which leave the team entirely? Apply it to your own team's workload.
exercises.rubric: Passes if the split keeps pipeline-cli at exactly one repo, assigns cross-project personal duties to a Level 2 agent, returns the dashboards to their owning team, and the learner maps at least one duty from their own context.

exercises.prompt: Dana's longer system prompt failed because more context always means more focus.
